# Crypto Events

Cryptographic problems are easy to miss when an application still appears to
work. A service can complete a request while quietly negotiating an obsolete TLS
protocol, using a legacy cipher suite, or depending on a certificate that is
close to expiry.

This example makes that problem visible with Java Flight Recorder (JFR). You
will run a small Java application that deliberately connects to
[badssl.com](https://badssl.com/) with **TLSv1.1**, capture the relevant JFR
security events, and inspect the recording from three angles:

- command-line analysis with `jfr print`
- visual inspection in JDK Mission Control (JMC)
- automated analysis with a small Java program and Codex

**Do not use TLSv1.1 in production. It is intentionally used here because it
gives the recording an obvious security issue to find.**

**References**

- [Monitoring Java Application Security with JDK tools and JFR Events](https://dev.java/learn/security/monitor/)
- [BadSSL.COM source code](https://github.com/chromium/badssl.com/)
- [badssl.com](https://badssl.com/)

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- [`jq`](https://jqlang.org/)

- [`codex`](https://developers.openai.com/codex/)

- [JDK Mission Control (JMC)](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/products-jmc9-downloads.html)

## JDK Mission Control (JMC)

1. Download the latest version of JMC from
   [here](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/products-jmc9-downloads.html)

2. Specify the version of Java

   When having multiple versions of Java installed, you may need to specify
   which one to be used by JMC. This can be done through the `jmc.ini` file,
   found under the `Eclipse` directory of where JMC is installed.

   Add the `-vm` option followed by the path to the `bin` directory, as shown
   next.

   ```
   ...
   -vm
   /Users/aattard/.sdkman/candidates/java/current/bin
   ...
   ```

   Please note that this file will contain other information, which is excluded
   for brevity.

## Build the application

The following examples require the application to be built.

```shell
./mvnw clean package
```

(*Optional*) Verify that the JAR file was created

```shell
tree --sort=name './target/libs'
```

There should be one JAR file

```
./target/libs
└── crypto-events-1.0.0.jar

1 directory, 1 file
```

Some of the following commands dump JFR files into a `jfr` directory. Make sure
that the `jfr` directory exists.

```shell
rm -rf './jfr'
mkdir -p './jfr'
```

## Create custom configuration

This example will analyse TLS handshakes and x509 certificates, which events are
not collected by either the *default* nor the *profile* configurations. This
provides insight on the protocols used and from where these were used. Create a
new configuration that captures these events.

1. Create the custom configuration

   ```shell
   jfr configure \
     jdk.TLSHandshake#enabled=true \
     jdk.TLSHandshake#stackTrace=true \
     jdk.X509Certificate#enabled=true \
     jdk.X509Validation#enabled=true \
     --output './jfr/custom.jfc'
   ```

   Unfortunately, this cannot be enabled using the `jfr configure --interactive`
   option.

2. (*Optional*) A `.jfc` file will be created. This file can be saved anywhere
   on the filesystem as long as it is accessible. For this example, the `.jfc`
   is saved under the `jfr` directory.

   ```shell
   tree --sort=name './jfr'
   ```

   The custom configuration

   ```
   ./jfr
   └── custom.jfc

   1 directory, 1 file
   ```

   The `.jfr` file is an XML file and can be viewed and edited manually.

## Analyse Crypto Events

1. Run the application and capture the recordings using the custom configuration

   ```shell
   java \
     -Djava.security.properties="file://$(pwd)/config/java.weak.security" \
     -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=30s,delay=5s,name='Crypto',filename='./jfr/demo.jfr',settings='./jfr/custom.jfc' \
     -jar './target/libs/crypto-events-1.0.0.jar'
   ```

   Alternatively, you can enable the `jdk.TLSHandshake` and
   `jdk.X509Certificate` JFR events from the command line.

   ```shell
   java \
     -Djava.security.properties="file://$(pwd)/config/java.weak.security" \
     -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=30s,delay=5s,name='Crypto',filename='./jfr/demo.jfr',jdk.TLSHandshake#enabled=true,jdk.TLSHandshake#stackTrace=true,jdk.X509Certificate#enabled=true,jdk.X509Validation#enabled=true \
     -jar './target/libs/crypto-events-1.0.0.jar'
   ```

2. Analyse the TLS handshake events

   The `jfr` command can be used to analyse the recordings from the command
   line.

   Print a summary of the events observed and their frequency

   ```shell
   jfr summary './jfr/demo.jfr' | grep 'jdk.TLSHandshake'
   ```

   The number of TLS Handshake events raised during the recording

   ```
    jdk.TLSHandshake                            6           214
   ```

   Print the events in JSON format and use the `jq` command to format it and
   limit to the first event, otherwise all `jdk.TLSHandshake` will be printed.

   ```shell
   jfr print --json --events 'jdk.TLSHandshake' './jfr/demo.jfr' | jq '.recording.events[0]'
   ```

   At the bottom of the event you can see the protocol used, which is the
   insecure `TLSv1.1`.

   ```
    jdk.X509Certificate                        18          1472
   ```

   Print the events in JSON format and use the `jq` command to format it and

   printed.

   ```shell
   jfr print --json --events 'jdk.X509Certificate' './jfr/demo.jfr' | jq '.recording.events[0]'
   ```

5. Analyse the recording file (`./jfr/demo.jfr`) with a custom program

   A Java program can open the JFR recording file and analyse each event. The
   following example reads the recording file, filters for
   `jdk.X509Certificate`, and analyses the certificate. A warning is displayed
   if the certificate is nearing expiry. While this example is kept simple, the
   program can be extended to perform more advanced actions.

   ```java
   #!/usr/bin/env -S java --source 25

   import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedEvent;
   import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingFile;

   import static java.util.Objects.requireNonNull;

   void main(final String[] args) {
       if (args.length != 1) {
           System.err.println("Usage: ./PrintCertificateState <RECORDING-FILE>");
           System.exit(1);
       }

       final Map<Long, CertificateState> results = compute(Path.of(args[0]));

       results.forEach((id, state) -> {
           switch (state) {
               case BEFORE_VALID_FROM -> IO.println("Certificate with id " + id + " is not yet active");
               case WILL_EXPIRED_IN_LESS_THAN_90_DAYS ->
                       IO.println("Certificate with id " + id + " will expire in less than 90 days");
               case WILL_EXPIRED_IN_LESS_THAN_30_DAYS ->
                       IO.println("Certificate with id " + id + " will expire in less than 30 days");
               case WILL_EXPIRED_IN_LESS_THAN_7_DAYS ->
                       IO.println("Certificate with id " + id + " will expire in less than 7 days");
               case EXPIRED -> IO.println("Certificate with id " + id + " is expired");
               case VALID -> IO.println("Certificate with id " + id + " is valid");
           }
       });
   }

   private static Map<Long, CertificateState> compute(final Path path) {
       final Map<Long, CertificateState> results = new HashMap<>();

       try (RecordingFile recordingFile = new RecordingFile(path)) {
           while (recordingFile.hasMoreEvents()) {
               final RecordedEvent event = recordingFile.readEvent();

               if ("jdk.X509Certificate".equals(event.getEventType().getName())) {
                   final long certificateId = event.getValue("certificateId");
                   results.computeIfAbsent(certificateId, key -> CertificateState.of(event));
               }
           }

           return results;
       } catch (final IOException e) {
           throw new UncheckedIOException("Failed to read recording file " + path, e);
       }
   }

   private enum CertificateState {

       BEFORE_VALID_FROM,
       EXPIRED,
       WILL_EXPIRED_IN_LESS_THAN_7_DAYS,
       WILL_EXPIRED_IN_LESS_THAN_30_DAYS,
       WILL_EXPIRED_IN_LESS_THAN_90_DAYS,
       VALID;

       public static CertificateState of(final RecordedEvent event) {
           requireNonNull(event);

           final String eventName = event.getEventType().getName();
           if (!"jdk.X509Certificate".equals(eventName)) {
               throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid event type " + eventName);
           }

           final LocalDateTime validFrom = getValidFromLocalDateTime(event);
           final LocalDateTime validUntil = getValidUntilLocalDateTime(event);
           final LocalDateTime referenceDate = LocalDateTime.now();

           return of(validFrom, validUntil, referenceDate);
       }

       public static CertificateState of(final LocalDateTime validFrom, final LocalDateTime validUntil, final LocalDateTime referenceDate) {
           requireNonNull(validFrom);
           requireNonNull(validUntil);
           requireNonNull(referenceDate);

           if (validFrom.isAfter(validUntil)) {
               throw new IllegalArgumentException("The valid from date (" + validFrom + ") cannot be after the valid until date (" + validUntil + ')');
           }

           if (referenceDate.isBefore(validFrom)) {
               return BEFORE_VALID_FROM;
           }

           if (referenceDate.isAfter(validUntil)) {
               return EXPIRED;
           }

           final long daysToExpire = ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(referenceDate, validUntil);
           if (daysToExpire < 7) {return WILL_EXPIRED_IN_LESS_THAN_7_DAYS;}
           if (daysToExpire < 30) {return WILL_EXPIRED_IN_LESS_THAN_30_DAYS;}
           if (daysToExpire < 90) {return WILL_EXPIRED_IN_LESS_THAN_90_DAYS;}

           return VALID;
       }

       private static LocalDateTime getValidFromLocalDateTime(final RecordedEvent event) {
           return getLocalDateTime(event, "validFrom");
       }

       private static LocalDateTime getValidUntilLocalDateTime(final RecordedEvent event) {
           return getLocalDateTime(event, "validUntil");
       }

       private static LocalDateTime getLocalDateTime(final RecordedEvent event, final String name) {
           return LocalDateTime.ofInstant(Instant.ofEpochMilli(event.getValue(name)), ZONE_ID);
       }

       private static final ZoneId ZONE_ID = ZoneId.systemDefault();
   }
   ```

   Run the program with our recording.

   ```shell
   ./src/main/java/PrintCertificateState './jfr/demo.jfr'
   ```

   The program will print a message similar to the following

   ```
   Certificate with id 1195325897 will expire in less than 90 days
   Certificate with id 2676876522 is valid
   Certificate with id 1464082652 is valid
   ```

6. Analyse the recording with AI

   A model should not be given the recording blindly. The JFR file is the source
   of truth, and the model is used to explain selected evidence extracted from
   it. The following command extracts the security-relevant events, stores the
   reduced input under `./jfr/crypto-events-for-ai.json`, and asks Codex to
   analyse that evidence.

   ```shell
   # Run Codex from an isolated directory so it can only see the files provided for this analysis
   rm -rf 'target/jfr-1'
   mkdir -p 'target/jfr-1'

   # Extract the events of interest and keep only the fields relevant to the prompt
   jfr print --json \
     --events 'jdk.TLSHandshake,jdk.X509Certificate,jdk.X509Validation' \
     './jfr/demo.jfr' |
     jq '{
       events: [
         .recording.events[] | {
           type,
           startTime: .values.startTime,
           peerHost: .values.peerHost,
           peerPort: .values.peerPort,
           protocolVersion: .values.protocolVersion,
           cipherSuite: .values.cipherSuite,
           certificateId: .values.certificateId,
           subject: .values.subject,
           issuer: .values.issuer,
           keyType: .values.keyType,
           keyLength: .values.keyLength,
           validFrom: .values.validFrom,
           validUntil: .values.validUntil,
           certificatePosition: .values.certificatePosition,
           validationCounter: .values.validationCounter
         }
       ]
     }' > 'target/jfr-1/crypto-events-for-ai.json'

   # Analyse the extracted JSON file
   codex exec \
     --ephemeral \
     --cd "${PWD}/target/jfr-1" \
     --sandbox read-only \
     --model gpt-6.1-terra \
     --config 'model_reasoning_effort="medium"' \
     --skip-git-repo-check \
     --output-last-message 'target/crypto-events-ai-analysis-1.md' \
     - <<'EOF' > 'target/jfr-1/crypto-events-ai-run.log' 2>&1
   You are analysing Java Flight Recorder security events for a workshop.

   Read `crypto-events-for-ai.json`. Use only the supplied JFR-derived evidence. Do not invent events.

   Identify:
   1. insecure TLS protocol usage
   2. weak or notable cipher suites
   3. certificate expiry risks
   4. certificate validation activity
   5. what a workshop participant should inspect in JDK Mission Control

   Return a concise finding list with evidence fields.
   EOF
   ```

   Alternatively, delegate the whole analysis to the model. This is less
   deterministic than extracting the evidence first, but it demonstrates how an
   agent can inspect the recording and decide which JDK tools to use.

   ```shell
   # Run Codex from an isolated directory so it can only see the files provided for this analysis
   rm -rf 'target/jfr-2'
   mkdir -p 'target/jfr-2'

   # Copy the recording
   cp 'jfr/demo.jfr' 'target/jfr-2/demo.jfr'

   # Delegate the whole analysis to the model
   codex exec \
     --ephemeral \
     --cd "${PWD}/target/jfr-2" \
     --sandbox read-only \
     --model gpt-6.1-terra \
     --config 'model_reasoning_effort="medium"' \
     --skip-git-repo-check \
     --output-last-message 'target/crypto-events-ai-analysis-2.md' \
     - <<'EOF' > 'target/jfr-2/crypto-events-ai-run.log' 2>&1
   You are analysing Java Flight Recorder security events for a workshop.
   ```

   - The second result where the model recived and analysed the actual JFR
     recording: `target/crypto-events-ai-analysis-1.md`

     ```markdown
     Analysed only `demo.jfr` using `jfr summary` and `jfr print`. Recording: **2026-10-09, 10:16:20 UTC, 30 seconds**.

     1. **Insecure TLS protocol observed.** All **6 `jdk.TLSHandshake` events** negotiated TLS 1.1.
        - Evidence: `peerHost=tls-v1-1.badssl.com`, `peerPort=1011`, `protocolVersion=TLSv1.1`, `certificateId=1195325897`.
        - First/last: `10:16:21.164` / `10:16:47.563` UTC.
        - Supporting configuration: recorded `jdk.tls.disabledAlgorithms` omits `TLSv1.1`.

     2. **Legacy cipher suite observed in all 6 handshakes.**
        - Evidence: `cipherSuite=TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA`.
        - Notable properties: AES-256 in CBC mode with HMAC-SHA1; ECDHE provides forward secrecy. The concern is the legacy CBC/SHA1 construction alongside TLS 1.1; AES-256 itself is not a weak key size.

     3. **No expired certificate observed; leaf renewal is the nearest expiry concern.**
        - Evidence: `jdk.X509Certificate`, `certificateId=1195325897`, `subject=CN=*.badssl.com`, `issuer=CN=YR1, O=Let's Encrypt, C=US`.
        - Validity: `2026-09-29 20:02:56` → **`2026-12-28 20:02:55 UTC`**, approximately **80 days remaining** at recording time.
        - Other observed certificates expire `2028-09-02` (YR1, ID `2676876522`) and `2032-09-02` (Root YR, ID `1464082652`).
        - The **18 certificate events represent 3 distinct certificate IDs**, each recorded six times.

     4. **Repeated PKIX certificate validation activity recorded.**
        - Evidence: **24 `jdk.X509Validation` events**, `validationCounter=1–6`, each containing `certificatePosition=1–4`; thread `main`; stack includes `PKIXCertPathValidator.validate`.
        - Position → certificate ID: `1→1521974916`, `2→1464082652`, `3→2676876522`, `4→1195325897`.
        - Each group precedes a recorded handshake. ID `1521974916` has no matching certificate-detail event, so its identity and expiry cannot be established from this recording. These fields do not independently establish hostname or revocation checks.

     5. **In JDK Mission Control, inspect these event types and fields.**
        - `jdk.TLSHandshake`: host/port, protocol, cipher, timestamp and certificate ID.
        - `jdk.X509Certificate`: correlate by certificate ID; inspect subject/issuer, validity, signature algorithm and key length.
        - `jdk.X509Validation`: group by validation counter, order by certificate position, and inspect timestamps, thread and stack traces.
        - `jdk.InitialSecurityProperty`: inspect `jdk.tls.disabledAlgorithms` to explain why TLS 1.1 was permitted.
     ```

   They should identify the same broad security issues, but the wording and
   supporting evidence may differ because one prompt receives curated event data
   while the other asks the agent to inspect the recording itself.

   The extracted-evidence approach is usually faster and uses fewer tokens
   because the model receives only the relevant JFR fields as plain text. The
   delegated approach is more flexible, but the agent has to decide how to
   inspect the JFR recording and convert the binary data into text before the
   model can reason about it.
